lessons.title: Types of Pumps: Manual, Solar, Petrol, and Electric
lessons.body: Choosing a pump starts with your water source, field size, and budget. The four main types for smallholders are manual, solar, petrol, and electric. Manual pumps include treadle pumps (like the MoneyMaker) and hand pumps. A treadle pump can lift water from 7 meters depth and deliver about 1,000 to 3,000 liters per hour. It costs $50â$150 and needs only human power. Use it for vegetable plots up to 0.2 hectares. Solar pumps use photovoltaic panels to power a DC submersible or surface pump. A 200-watt panel kit with a 12V pump can lift water 10 meters and deliver 1,500 liters per hour. Cost is $300â$800. They work best in sunny areas and need a battery or direct drive for daytime irrigation. Petrol pumps are portable and powerful. A 2-inch petrol pump (e.g., Honda WB20) moves 600 liters per minute at 30 meters head. Fuel consumption is about 0.5 liters per hour. Cost $200â$400. Use for larger fields or when you need high flow. Electric pumps run on grid or generator power. A 1-horsepower (0.75 kW) electric pump delivers 3,000â5,000 liters per hour. They are quiet and cheap to run but need reliable electricity. Cost $150â$500 plus wiring. In Africa, solar is often best for remote areas, petrol for mobility, and electric where grid power is stable. Match pump type to your water depth, required flow, and available energy.

lessons.title: Sizing a Pump for Your Irrigation System
lessons.body: Sizing a pump means matching its flow rate (liters per minute, L/min) and head (total vertical lift plus friction loss) to your crop needs. First, calculate your peak water requirement. For a 0.5-hectare maize field in dry season, you need about 5 mm of water per day. That equals 5 liters per square meter per day. 0.5 ha = 5,000 mÂ², so 25,000 liters per day. If you irrigate for 4 hours, you need 6,250 L/hour, or about 104 L/min. Next, measure total head. Head = vertical lift (from water surface to highest point of irrigation) + friction loss in pipes. For every 10 meters of 1-inch pipe, friction loss is about 0.5 meters. If you lift 5 meters and have 20 meters of pipe, total head = 5 + (20/10)*0.5 = 6 meters. Then add pressure needed at the outlet (e.g., 5 meters for sprinklers). Total head = 11 meters. Now choose a pump that delivers 104 L/min at 11 meters head. Check the pump curve: a 1-inch petrol pump might give 120 L/min at 10 meters headâgood. A solar pump with 200W panel might give 80 L/min at 10 metersâtoo low. Oversizing wastes fuel or electricity; undersizing starves crops. Always add 20% safety margin. For drip irrigation, you need lower flow but higher pressure (10â15 meters). For sprinklers, higher flow (200â400 L/min per hectare) and 20â30 meters head. Use a bucket and stopwatch to measure your actual flow from a pump: fill a 20-liter bucket, time it, then calculate L/min. That tells you if the pump meets your design.

lessons.title: Solar-Powered Pumping Systems for Smallholds
lessons.body: Solar pumps are ideal for Africa: no fuel, low maintenance, and the sun is free. A basic system has four parts: solar panels, a controller, a pump (submersible or surface), and piping. For a smallholder, a 200W to 500W panel array is common. A 300W panel can power a 12V or 24V DC pump that lifts water from 10 meters and delivers 1,500â3,000 liters per hour. Cost: $400â$1,200 for a complete kit. Install panels facing north (in southern hemisphere) or south (in northern hemisphere) at an angle equal to your latitude. In Kenya (latitude 0Â°), tilt panels 10Â° for best year-round output. Use a controller with MPPT (Maximum Power Point Tracking) to boost efficiency by 20â30%. Connect panels to the controller, then to the pump. For submersible pumps, lower the pump into a borehole or well, keeping it at least 1 meter above the bottom to avoid silt. For surface pumps, place them beside a river or tank. A float switch prevents dry running. Solar pumps work best during sunny hours (9amâ4pm). You can store water in a tank for evening irrigation. A 5,000-liter tank fills in 2â3 hours with a 2,000 L/h pump. Maintenance: clean panels weekly with a soft cloth and water; check wiring for corrosion; inspect pump intake for debris. In cloudy weather, output drops 50â70%, so size your system for the worst month. Solar pumps have no fuel cost, but initial cost is higher. Over 3 years, they often beat petrol pumps on total cost.

lessons.title: Maintenance and Troubleshooting of Small Pumps
lessons.body: Regular maintenance prevents breakdowns and extends pump life. For petrol pumps: check oil level daily (use SAE 10W-30), clean air filter every 50 hours, replace spark plug every 100 hours, and clean fuel filter monthly. For solar pumps: clean panels weekly, check controller lights for errors, and inspect wiring for loose connections. For electric pumps: check voltage (should be within 10% of rated), tighten terminal screws, and listen for unusual noises. For manual pumps: grease moving parts monthly and replace worn leather seals yearly. Common problems and fixes: Pump won't start â check fuel (petrol), battery charge (solar), or power supply (electric). If petrol engine turns but won't fire, clean spark plug and check fuel flow. Low flow â check for clogged intake screen, worn impeller, or air leaks in suction pipe. For solar, low flow often means dirty panels or a failing controller. Overheating â ensure pump has clear ventilation and not running dry. Dry running damages seals; install a float switch or run pump only when water is available. Leaks â tighten fittings, replace O-rings, use Teflon tape on threads. Noise or vibration â check mounting bolts, align pump with motor, and remove debris from impeller. Keep a spare parts kit: spark plug, air filter, fuel filter, impeller, seals, and a multimeter. In Africa, dust and heat are hard on pumps. Store petrol pumps under cover. For solar, protect controller from rain. If a pump fails, first check the simplest things: fuel, power, blockage. Many 'broken' pumps just need a clean spark plug or a cleared intake. If unsure, call a local technician. Preventive maintenance costs 10% of repair costs.

lessons.title: Fuel and Energy Efficiency for Pumping
lessons.body: Pumping water costs moneyâeither fuel or electricity. To cut costs, focus on efficiency. For petrol pumps: use the correct fuel-oil mix for 2-stroke (50:1) or straight petrol for 4-stroke. Keep the engine tuned: a dirty air filter can increase fuel use by 20%. Run the pump at its optimal speedâusually 3,000â3,600 RPM. Don't oversize: a 2-inch pump using 1.5 L/hour to move 600 L/min is efficient; a 3-inch pump using 3 L/hour for the same flow wastes fuel. Use a larger suction hose (2-inch instead of 1.5-inch) to reduce friction. For solar pumps: maximize panel output by cleaning them daily and adjusting tilt seasonally. Use MPPT controllers. Avoid shadingâeven a small shadow on one panel can cut output by 50%. For electric pumps: use high-efficiency motors (IE3 or IE4). Replace standard V-belts with cogged belts to save 2â5%. Reduce pipe friction by using larger diameter pipes and smooth bends. For all pumps: match pump flow to irrigation demand. If you pump more water than needed, you waste energy. Use a tank to store water during off-peak hours (for electric) or sunny hours (for solar). For petrol, buy fuel in bulk to reduce cost. In Africa, fuel prices vary; a pump using 0.5 L/hour at $1.50/L costs $0.75/hour. If you pump 4 hours daily, that's $3/day, $90/month. Solar has zero fuel cost. A solar pump costing $800 pays back in 9 months compared to petrol. Also, regular maintenance saves fuel: a clogged air filter or worn spark plug can increase consumption by 30%. Keep records of fuel use and water pumped to spot inefficiencies.

lessons.title: Safety Practices for Pump Operation
lessons.body: Pumps can be dangerous if not handled properly. Follow these safety rules to avoid injury and damage. For petrol pumps: always refuel outdoors, away from flames. Petrol is highly flammable. Let the engine cool before refueling. Never smoke near fuel. Store fuel in approved containers, away from children. Exhaust fumes contain carbon monoxideânever run a petrol pump in an enclosed space. For electric pumps: ensure proper grounding (earth wire). Use an RCD (residual current device) to prevent shocks. Keep electrical connections dry. Never touch a pump with wet hands. For solar pumps: panels produce DC electricity during daylightâcover panels with a cloth before working on wiring. The controller can hold charge; disconnect panels first. For manual pumps: use proper lifting technique when moving heavy parts. Wear gloves to avoid blisters. For all pumps: wear safety goggles when working on impellers or pressure lines. Never put hands near moving parts. Before maintenance, switch off power (electric), turn off fuel (petrol), or cover panels (solar). Release pressure from pipes before opening. Use a pressure gauge to check. Keep children and animals away from pump area. Secure hoses to prevent whipping if they disconnect. Use clamps, not wire. For submersible pumps: use a safety rope when loweringânever lift by the cable. Check that the well is not contaminated by fuel or oil. In case of fuel spill, contain it with sand and dispose properly. First aid: for cuts, clean and bandage. For electric shock, turn off power before touching victim. For fuel on skin, wash with soap. Always have a fire extinguisher (dry powder) near petrol pumps. Train all operators on safe start-up and shut-down procedures. Safety is not optionalâit saves lives.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pumps and Power Units for Smallholder Irrigation in Africa

This practical reference consolidates the core technical, financial, and safety knowledge a smallholder farmer or agribusiness service provider needs to select, size, operate, and maintain an irrigation pump. It is written for the African context, where fuel costs, unreliable grid electricity, and limited access to spare parts shape every decision. The goal is simple: get water to the crop at the lowest cost per cubic metre, with equipment that can be repaired locally and operated safely by the people on the farm.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, smallholder irrigation is expanding rapidly. The African Development Bank estimates that less than 10% of cultivated land in Africa is irrigated, compared with over 40% in Asia, yet irrigation can raise yields by 50â300% and reduce drought risk. Pumps are the heart of any irrigation system, and choosing the wrong pump â or running the right pump badly â is one of the most common and expensive mistakes. A poorly sized petrol pump can waste 30â50% of its fuel, while a solar pump mismatched to the borehole can fail to fill a tank before nightfall.

1. Types of Pumps: Matching the Pump to the Farm

There are four practical pump categories for smallholders in Africa: manual, solar, petrol, and electric. Each has a distinct cost structure, maintenance profile, and best-fit use case.

Table 1: Comparison of pump types for smallholder irrigation in Africa
Pump type Typical capital cost (USD) Running cost Best-fit use case Key limitation
Manual (treadle, rope-and-washer, hand) 50â250 Labour only 0.1â0.5 ha, shallow wells <10 m, vegetable plots Low flow, high labour, fatigue
Solar (submersible or surface) 600â3,500 Near zero (panel cleaning) 0.5â3 ha, boreholes 10â80 m, daytime irrigation High upfront cost, no night pumping without battery
Petrol (centrifugal, 2â6.5 HP) 150â600 Fuel 1.5â3 L/hr, oil, spark plugs 1â5 ha, portable, river/pond suction lift <7 m Fuel price volatility, noise, CO emissions
Electric (AC centrifugal or submersible) 200â1,200 Grid tariff or diesel generator fuel 1â10 ha where grid is reliable Requires grid or generator; voltage fluctuations

Sources: Adapted from FAO, Small-scale irrigation pumping systems (Land and Water Division); and the African Development Bank, Feed Africa: Strategy for Agricultural Transformation in Africa (2016â2025). Costs are indicative 2024 market ranges for Kenya, Ghana, and Zambia.

2. Sizing a Pump for Your Irrigation System

Pump sizing is a business decision, not just an engineering one. An oversized pump costs more to buy and run; an undersized pump fails to meet crop water demand at peak. The three variables that matter are flow rate (Q), total head (H), and power (P).

Step 1 â Crop water requirement. Estimate peak daily water demand. For vegetables in East Africa, a common planning figure is 4â6 mm/day, rising to 7 mm/day in hot dry spells. One hectare at 5 mm/day needs 50 mÂ³/day, or about 50,000 litres. If you irrigate 4 hours per day, that is 12.5 mÂ³/hr (about 12,500 L/hr).

Step 2 â Total head. Total head = static lift (vertical distance from water level to outlet) + friction losses in pipes and fittings + discharge pressure. A simple rule: add 10â20% to static lift for friction in a well-designed system, more if pipes are long or narrow.

Step 3 â Power. Use the hydraulic power formula:

P (kW) = (Q Ã H Ã Ï Ã g) / (3,600,000 Ã Î·)

Where Q is in mÂ³/hr, H in metres, Ï = 1000 kg/mÂ³, g = 9.81 m/sÂ², and Î· is pump efficiency (typically 0.4â0.6 for small petrol pumps, 0.5â0.7 for solar submersibles). A practical shortcut: kW â (Q Ã H) / 367 / Î· with Q in mÂ³/hr.

Table 2: Indicative pump sizing examples for smallholder plots (Africa, 2024 costs)
Plot size / crop Peak demand (mÂ³/day) Static lift (m) Recommended pump Indicative cost (USD)
0.25 ha vegetables, treadle 12â15 5â8 Manual treadle pump 80â200
0.5 ha vegetables, solar 25â30 15â25 0.5â1 HP solar submersible + 300 W panel 700â1,200
1 ha maize/vegetables, petrol 50â60 8â12 3 HP petrol centrifugal 350â600
2 ha mixed, solar 90â120 30â50 2â3 HP solar submersible + 1.5 kW array 2,000â3,500
3 ha, electric (grid) 150â180 20â40 5 HP AC submersible 800â1,500

Sources: FAO, Irrigation Water Management: Irrigation Methods (Training Manual No. 5); and Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO), Irrigation Technology Options for Smallholders (2021). Costs are indicative and vary by country and supplier.

3. Solar-Powered Pumping Systems for Smallholds

Solar pumping is the fastest-growing irrigation technology in Africa because it eliminates fuel costs and grid dependence. A typical smallholder system has four components: the solar array, the controller (often MPPT), the pump (submersible or surface), and the storage tank or direct drip lines.

Business case. A 1 HP solar submersible costing about USD 1,000 can replace a petrol pump that uses 1.5 L/hr at USD 1.20/L. Over a 4-hour daily pumping season of 200 days, that is USD 1,440 per year in fuel alone â the solar system pays back in under a year. After that, the marginal cost of water is nearly zero, which transforms the economics of high-value horticulture.

Design rules. (1) Size the array for the worst month (lowest irradiance), not the best. (2) Use a storage tank of at least one day's demand so irrigation is not interrupted by clouds. (3) Keep the pump within its efficiency range â running a solar pump at low sun is inefficient. (4) Protect panels from theft and livestock with a fence and, where possible, mount them on a roof or elevated frame.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â ELECTRICAL AND SOLAR PUMP HAZARDS

Solar arrays produce DC electricity whenever exposed to light â even when the controller is switched off. Never disconnect DC cables under load; arc flash can cause severe burns. Always cover panels with an opaque sheet before working on wiring. Submersible pump cables must be properly sealed and earthed; a damaged cable in water can be lethal. Only qualified technicians should open controllers or make electrical connections. For petrol pumps, never refuel a hot engine, never run indoors or in a closed shed (carbon monoxide kills silently), and keep a dry-powder fire extinguisher within 5 m of the pump. In all cases, keep children and untrained workers away from the pump station.

4. Maintenance and Troubleshooting of Small Pumps

Most pump failures in smallholder systems are preventable. The three most common causes are dirty fuel, worn impellers/seals, and dry running. A simple maintenance routine â daily checks, weekly cleaning, and an annual service â can double pump life.

Daily: check fuel/oil levels (petrol), check for leaks, listen for unusual noise, and record hours run. Weekly: clean the suction strainer, check panel cleanliness (solar), inspect cables and connections. Seasonally: change engine oil and spark plug (petrol), replace worn impeller or seals, flush the tank, and test the controller settings.

Common faults and fixes: Pump runs but no water â check suction lift, prime the pump, check for air leaks. Pump overheats â check for blocked impeller, low voltage, or dry running. Solar pump stops at midday â check controller fault codes, panel shading, or pump overload. Petrol engine won't start â check fuel, spark plug, air filter, and choke setting.

5. Fuel and Energy Efficiency for Pumping

Energy is often the largest recurring cost in smallholder irrigation. Efficiency measures that pay back fastest include: matching pump size to actual head and flow (avoid oversized pumps), using larger-diameter pipes to cut friction, eliminating unnecessary bends and valves, keeping suction lines short, and irrigating at night or early morning (for electric pumps) to reduce evaporation and, where tariffs allow, use off-peak power.

For petrol pumps, the single biggest saving is correct carburettor tuning and clean air filters â a dirty filter can increase fuel consumption by 10â15%. For solar, the biggest saving is panel cleaning and correct tilt; dusty panels in the Sahel can lose 20â30% of output. For electric pumps, power factor correction and correct cable sizing reduce losses.

6. Safety Practices for Pump Operation

Safety is a business issue: an injury stops irrigation, and a burnt pump stops income. Key practices: (1) never operate a petrol engine in an enclosed space; (2) keep fuel in approved containers away from the pump; (3) wear eye protection when priming or handling chemicals; (4) lock the pump house and controller cabinet; (5) train at least two people on the farm to operate and shut down the system; (6) keep a first-aid kit and fire extinguisher at the pump station; (7) for solar, treat all DC cables as live; (8) for electric, ensure proper earthing and use an RCD/earth leakage breaker.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Match pump to demand: calculate peak daily water need (mÂ³/day) and total head (m) before buying.
  • Size for the worst month: use dry-season crop demand, not average, and lowest solar irradiance for solar systems.
  • Check suction lift: petrol centrifugal pumps should not exceed 7 m suction lift; use submersibles for deeper water.
  • Protect the pump: install a strainer, non-return valve, and (for electric/solar) a dry-run protection device.
  • Maintain daily: check fuel, oil, leaks, noise, and panel cleanliness; record running hours.
  • Service annually: replace impeller, seals, spark plug, and engine oil before the peak season.
  • Train two operators: never rely on one person; keep a written start-up and shut-down procedure at the pump.
  • Prioritise safety: no refuelling hot engines, no indoor petrol operation, cover solar panels before wiring work, and keep a fire extinguisher and first-aid kit on site.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Land and Water: Irrigation and Water Management (free technical guides, including solar pumping and small-scale irrigation).
  • FAO â Solar-Powered Irrigation Systems: A Clean Energy Solution for Sustainable Agriculture (free PDF, 2018).
  • GIZ â Solar Water Pumping for Irrigation (free PDF, 2019).
  • African Development Bank â Feed Africa Strategy 2016â2025 (free PDF, irrigation and agricultural transformation).
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (free irrigation technology and crop guides for smallholders).

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course Irrigation Systems for Smallholds. Always verify local prices, regulations, and equipment availability with your national agricultural extension service or a certified irrigation supplier before purchase or installation.

quiz.q: Which pump type is best for a remote area with no grid electricity and limited budget?
quiz.explanation: Manual treadle pumps are cheapest and need no fuel or electricity, ideal for small plots.

quiz.q: What is the typical flow rate of a treadle pump?
quiz.explanation: A treadle pump delivers about 1,000 to 3,000 liters per hour.

quiz.q: Which pump type requires a battery or direct drive for daytime irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Solar pumps either use batteries or run directly during sunny hours.

quiz.q: A 2-inch petrol pump like Honda WB20 typically moves how much water?
quiz.explanation: The Honda WB20 moves about 600 liters per minute at 30 meters head.

quiz.q: What is the first step in sizing a pump?
quiz.explanation: You must know how much water your crops need before choosing a pump.

quiz.q: For a 0.5-hectare maize field needing 5 mm water per day, how many liters per day are needed?
quiz.explanation: 5 mm over 5,000 mÂ² equals 5 L/mÂ² Ã 5,000 = 25,000 L.

quiz.q: What is total head in pump sizing?
options: B) Vertical lift plus friction loss plus pressure needed
quiz.explanation: Total head includes lift, friction loss in pipes, and required outlet pressure.

quiz.q: If you lift water 5 meters and have 20 meters of 1-inch pipe (friction loss 0.5 m per 10 m), what is the friction loss?
quiz.explanation: 20 m pipe gives 20/10 Ã 0.5 = 1.0 m friction loss.

quiz.q: Why add a 20% safety margin when sizing a pump?
options: A) To account for future expansion and wear
C) To make the pump heavier
quiz.explanation: A safety margin ensures the pump meets demand even with wear or unexpected needs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended tilt for solar panels in Kenya (latitude 0Â°)?
quiz.explanation: At the equator, a 10Â° tilt gives good year-round output.

quiz.q: What does MPPT stand for in solar pump controllers?
quiz.explanation: MPPT maximizes power output from solar panels.

quiz.q: How often should you clean solar panels?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning keeps dust from reducing output.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of low flow in a petrol pump?
quiz.explanation: A clogged intake screen restricts water flow.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid running a pump dry?
quiz.explanation: Dry running overheats and damages pump seals.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to measure actual pump flow?
quiz.explanation: Fill a 20-liter bucket and time it to calculate L/min.

quiz.q: How often should you replace the spark plug in a petrol pump?
quiz.explanation: Spark plugs typically last about 100 hours of operation.

quiz.q: What should you do before working on a solar pump's wiring?
options: A) Cover panels with a cloth
quiz.explanation: Covering panels stops electricity generation for safe work.

quiz.q: Which of these increases fuel consumption in a petrol pump?
quiz.explanation: A dirty air filter can increase fuel use by 20%.

quiz.q: What is the payback period for a $800 solar pump compared to petrol if petrol costs $90/month?
quiz.explanation: $800 Ã· $90/month â 8.9 months, about 9 months.

quiz.q: Why use a larger suction hose?
quiz.explanation: Larger diameter reduces friction loss, improving efficiency.

quiz.q: What safety device prevents electric shock?
quiz.explanation: An RCD (residual current device) cuts power if a fault is detected.

quiz.q: Where should you refuel a petrol pump?
quiz.explanation: Petrol fumes are flammable; refuel outdoors away from ignition sources.

quiz.q: What should you do if fuel spills?
options: B) Contain with sand and dispose properly
quiz.explanation: Sand absorbs fuel, preventing environmental contamination and fire.

quiz.q: Why should you never run a petrol pump in an enclosed space?
options: C) It uses too much fuel
quiz.explanation: Exhaust fumes contain carbon monoxide, which can be fatal.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check if a petrol pump won't start?
quiz.explanation: Always check the simplest things first: fuel, spark, air.

quiz.q: How often should you grease moving parts of a manual pump?
quiz.explanation: Monthly greasing keeps manual pumps operating smoothly.

quiz.q: What is a good preventive maintenance schedule for a solar pump controller?
quiz.explanation: Checking controller lights weekly helps spot errors early.

quiz.q: Which pump type has zero fuel cost?
quiz.explanation: Solar pumps use free sunlight, so no fuel cost.

quiz.q: What is the recommended safety margin when sizing a pump?
quiz.explanation: A 20% margin accounts for wear, friction, and future needs.

quiz.q: What should you wear when working on a pump impeller?
quiz.explanation: Safety goggles protect eyes from debris and splashes.
